lessons.title: What Is One Lakh?

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered how many things make one lakh?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Large numbers and rice
activities.body: Earlier, the country had about one lakh varieties of rice. Farmers used to preserve different varieties of seeds. A seed bank has collected about one hundred indigenous rice varieties. Commas make large numbers easier to read. The number 12,78,830 is read as twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty. Read the groups between commas slowly.
keyPoints: The country earlier had about one lakh rice varieties.
Commas make large numbers easier to read.
12,78,830 is read using lakh, thousand and hundred groups.
activities.explanation: Large numbers and rice variety counts both help us practise reading commas.

activities.prompt: A collection has 5 ten-thousands of rice seeds. How many thousands of seeds is that?
steps: The collection has 5 ten-thousands of seeds.
We need the number of thousands, and each ten-thousand equals 10 thousands.
So 5 x 10 = 50, which is 50 thousands.

activities.title: One Button, Many Presses
activities.body: Three calculators use different buttons. The Thoughtful Thousands adds 1000 with one press. The Tedious Tens adds 10 with one press. The Handy Hundreds adds 100 with one press. More presses build larger amounts. Creative Chitti can make a number in several ways. Systematic Sippy uses buttons from +1 to +100000 with as few clicks as possible.
keyPoints: The Thoughtful Thousands has a +1000 button.
The Tedious Tens has a +10 button.
The Handy Hundreds has a +100 button.
activities.explanation: Each calculator has a simple button rule, so count its presses carefully.

lessons.title: Lakhs, Crores and Arabs

activities.prompt: How do lakh, crore, and Arab help us read really big numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Large numbers in India
activities.body: India groups digits in a 3-2-2-2 pattern from the right. One lakh has five zeroes, and one crore has seven zeroes. One lakh is one hundred times one thousand. One crore is one hundred times one lakh. One arab is one hundred times one crore. The American system groups digits in a 3-3-3-3 pattern. The words lakh and crore come from Sanskrit.
keyPoints: One lakh has five zeroes.
One crore is one hundred times one lakh.
One arab is one hundred times one crore.
activities.explanation: These patterns help you read large numbers clearly.

activities.prompt: A shop has 300 thousand buttons. How many lakhs of buttons does it have?
steps: One lakh is one hundred times one thousand.
Divide the number of thousands by one hundred to find the number of lakhs: 300 / 100 = 3.
Therefore, the shop has 3 lakhs of buttons.

Therefore, the shop has {answer} lakhs of buttons.
gen.hint: One lakh is one hundred times one thousand.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

The clear reading is 9 arab 87 crore 65 lakhs 1 thousand and 234 because every group is included.

activities.title: Exact and Approximate Numbers
activities.body: Sometimes exact numbers are not needed, so an approximation is enough. Chintamani had exactly 76,068 people in 2011, but about 75,000 gives its size. activities.prompt: How can numbers show what we combine, add, or separate?

activities.title: Expressions and Their Terms
activities.body: Ruby’s expression has two terms: 6 × 5 and 3. Together, they mean three more than 6 × 5. The cost of four dosas at 23 rupees each is shown as 4 × 23. Another expression, 100 ÷ 2, shows the number of new two-kilogram packets. His total combines four existing packets with 100 ÷ 2 new packets. There is more than one way to pay 432 rupees.
keyPoints: Ruby’s expression has two terms.
6 × 5 and 3 mean three more than 6 × 5.
4 × 23 shows the cost of four dosas.
activities.explanation: These expressions connect real situations with numbers and terms.

lessons.title: Removing Brackets and Distributing Multiplication

activities.prompt: Can we make these tricky brackets disappear without changing the answer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Removing Brackets
activities.body: Brackets are removed by looking at the sign just before them. After a minus sign, change every sign inside the brackets. After a plus sign, keep every sign inside the brackets. For example, 500 – (250 – 100) becomes 500 – 250 + 100. This shows how signs change when brackets are removed.
keyPoints: A minus sign changes every inner sign.
A plus sign keeps every inner sign.
activities.explanation: The sign before the brackets tells you how to change the inner signs.

activities.prompt: There are 6 boxes. Each box contains 2 red marbles and 4 blue marbles. How many marbles are there in all?
steps: Each box contains 6 marbles altogether.
There are 6 equal boxes, so multiply the number in one box by the number of boxes.
6 x 6 = 36 marbles.

gen.template: There are {a} boxes. Each box contains {b} red marbles and {c} blue marbles. How many marbles are there in all?
steps: Each box contains {each} marbles altogether.
There are {a} equal boxes, so multiply the number in one box by the number of boxes.
{a} x {each} = {answer} marbles.
gen.hint: First find how many marbles are in one box, then multiply by the number of boxes.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A shop has 200 coins. It takes 40 coins and then 3 more. Which expression shows the coins left?
steps: Start with 200 – (40 + 3), because both amounts are removed.
The outer minus changes both inner signs, because brackets follow minus.
So 40 and 3 become negative, because each inner sign changes.
Thus, it becomes 200 – 40 – 3, with the same value.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Distributing Multiplication
activities.body: Multiplication can be distributed over a sum. The multiple of a sum is the same as the sum of the multiples. So 5 × (4 + 3) becomes 5 × 4 + 5 × 3. Also, 10 × 98 + 3 × 98 equals 13 × 98. These equalities help us work with multiplication.
keyPoints: Distribute 5 across 4 + 3.
The multiple of a sum equals the sum of multiples.
activities.explanation: Distributing multiplication keeps the expression equal while making the products visible.

activities.prompt: In 500 – (250 – 100), the sign of 250 becomes ______.
activities.hint: The minus sign before the brackets changes both inner signs.
activities.explanation: The minus sign makes 250 negative and 100 positive.

activities.prompt: Which expression has the same value as 100 – (15 + 56)?
activities.explanation: Removing the minus sign gives 100 – 15 – 56. Both expressions have the same value.

activities.prompt: Match each bracketed expression with its equal form.
activities.explanation: After a minus sign, change the inner signs. This gives each matching expression.

activities.title: Reading decimal place value
activities.body: Decimal place value helps you read numbers by place. The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractional parts. Each place value is ten times bigger than the place to its right. One-tenths come from dividing one into ten equal parts. One-hundredths come from dividing a tenth into ten parts. In 70.5, the 7 is in the tens place and the 5 is in the tenths place.
keyPoints: The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractional parts.
Each place value is ten times bigger than the place to its right.
One-tenths and one-hundredths are parts of a whole unit.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you read decimals clearly.

activities.body: A millimetre is a small length unit. One centimetre has the length of 10 millimetres. Multiply centimetres by 10 to get millimetres. Divide millimetres by 10 to get centimetres. One metre is 100 centimetres. One kilogram is a mass unit. It equals 1,000 grams. For money, 1 rupee equals 100 paise. These equalities help you change units.

1 kilogram = 1000 grams

activities.body: Letter-numbers give a short way to show relationships and patterns. Letters such as a and s can stand for numbers. The expression a + 3 shows Shabnam's age when a is Aftab's age. If a is 23, s is 26 years. Matchstick examples use 2 × n, while shopping costs use c × 35 + j × 60.

activities.title: Rules for Expressions
activities.body: Swapping lets you add two numbers in any order. Grouping lets you add numbers in a convenient group. Neither change alters an expression’s value. You can use brackets with a negative sign outside. Brackets can be removed appropriately. A multiple of a sum equals the sum of its multiples. Before adding, turn every multiplication term into a number. Algebraic expressions take values when you replace their letters.
keyPoints: Swap numbers in any order.
Group terms conveniently.
Keep the expression’s value.
activities.explanation: These rules help you simplify expressions without changing their value.

5 + 3 = 8, so Meena has 8 marbles.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Simplifying Algebraic Expressions

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how to make a long expression shorter without changing its value?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Simplifying Expressions
activities.body: A rectangle’s perimeter can start as length + breadth + length + breadth. Using l and b, we write p = l + b + l + b. Like terms have the same letter-numbers, so this becomes p = 2l + 2b. Both forms take the same values. Terms with different letter-numbers are unlike terms. Adding 5c, 3c and 10c uses the distributive property and gives 18c. Similarly, 4v + 3v gives 7v.
keyPoints: p = l + b + l + b becomes p = 2l + 2b.
Like terms have the same letter-numbers.
Unlike terms have different letter-numbers.
activities.explanation: You have spotted how to combine terms without changing the value.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Calendar and Matchstick Patterns

activities.prompt: Can you discover the calendar’s secret and predict how many matchsticks come next?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Calendar diagonals and matchstick patterns
activities.body: A diagonal means a slanting line. The marked calendar square has 12, 20, 13 and 19 on its diagonals. If a is the centre, its opposite number is 8 more. The number below is 7 more. Both diagonal sums equal 2a + 8. The five-number total is 5 times its centre. In the matchstick pattern, Step 5 needs 11 matchsticks. Each new step adds 2.
keyPoints: The two diagonal sums are equal.
The matchstick count is 3 + 2 × (y – 1).
This equals 2y + 1.
activities.explanation: These rules help you solve both calendar and matchstick patterns.

activities.prompt: The marked calendar square has 7, and the number diagonally opposite it is 8 greater. What is the diagonally opposite date number?
steps: The marked date number is 7.
The diagonally opposite date is 8 more, so 7 + 8 = 15.
The diagonally opposite date number is 15.

gen.template: The marked calendar square has {a}, and the number diagonally opposite it is 8 greater. What is the diagonally opposite date number?
steps: The marked date number is {a}.
The diagonally opposite date is 8 more, so {a} + 8 = {partner}.
The diagonally opposite date number is {answer}.
gen.hint: Start with the marked number and add 8.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A calendar shape uses a as one number. One diagonal adds a, a, and 8. What must the other diagonal add to match it?
steps: The first diagonal sum is a + a + 8, so it equals 2a + 8.
The other diagonal adds a + a + 1 + 7, so its extra parts are 1 and 7.
Because 1 and 7 together make 8, both sums equal 2a + 8.
So the diagonal sums are equal for any value of a.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which number is diagonally opposite 12?
activities.explanation: The marked diagonal pairs 12 with 20. This confirms the opposite number.

activities.prompt: The marked calendar square has 4, and the number directly below it is 7 greater. What is the date number below it?
activities.explanation: The marked date number is 4. The number below it is 7 more, so 4 + 7 = 11. The date number below it is 11.
steps: The marked date number is 4.
The number below it is 7 more, so 4 + 7 = 11.
The date number below it is 11.
activities.hint: Start with the marked number and add 7.

activities.prompt: In a marked calendar square, the number diagonally opposite 5 is 8 greater. What is the sum of the two date numbers on that diagonal?
activities.explanation: The marked date number is 5. The diagonally opposite number is 8 more, so it is 13. Adding the two numbers gives 5 + 13 = 18, so each diagonal sum is 18.
steps: The marked date number is 5.
The diagonally opposite number is 8 more, so it is 13.
Adding the two numbers gives 5 + 13 = 18, so each diagonal sum is 18.
activities.hint: First find the diagonally opposite number, and then add both diagonal numbers.

Adding the two numbers gives {a} + {opposite} = {answer}, so each diagonal sum is {answer}.

activities.prompt: A matchstick pattern uses 3 matchsticks at Step 1 and places 2 more matchsticks at each new step. How many matchsticks are needed at Step 5?
activities.explanation: Step 1 needs 3 matchsticks. By Step 5, there are 5 - 1 new steps, so the count is 3 + 2 x (5 - 1) = 11. Step 5 needs 11 matchsticks.
steps: Step 1 needs 3 matchsticks.
By Step 5, there are 5 - 1 new steps, so the count is 3 + 2 x (5 - 1) = 11.
Step 5 needs 11 matchsticks.
activities.hint: Start with 3 matchsticks and add 2 for every step after Step 1.

activities.prompt: At a market stall, a matchstick display uses 3 matchsticks for its first step and adds 2 matchsticks at each new step. If the display uses 9 matchsticks altogether, which step is it?
activities.explanation: The first step uses 3 matchsticks, and every new step adds 2. At Step 4, the count is 3 + 2 x (4 - 1) = 9. Because 6 = 2 x (4 - 1), the display is at Step 4.
steps: The first step uses 3 matchsticks, and every new step adds 2.
At Step 4, the count is 3 + 2 x (4 - 1) = 9.
Because 6 = 2 x (4 - 1), the display is at Step 4.
activities.hint: Subtract the first 3 matchsticks, then find how many additions of 2 were made.

activities.hint: Work through the matchstick formula.

activities.prompt: The marked calendar square has 5, and its diagonally opposite number is 8 greater. What is the sum of the two date numbers on that diagonal?
activities.explanation: The marked date number is 5. The diagonally opposite number is 8 more, so 5 + 8 = 13. Adding the two date numbers gives 5 + 13 = 18.

activities.prompt: The marked diagonals are 12 with 20 and 13 with 19. A child says equal sums need equal pairs. Why is this wrong?
options: The pairs differ, but both diagonal totals match.
The pairs must have equal numbers in every place.
Equal totals always make every number equal.
Different pairs can match only when a is small.

why.The pairs must have equal numbers in eve: This confuses equal sums with equal numbers in each pair.
why.Equal totals always make every number eq: This claims that equality applies to every number, not just the totals.
why.Different pairs can match only when a is: This adds a size condition, but the rule works for any value of a.

activities.explanation: Equal totals do not require every pair of numbers to be equal.

activities.prompt: One diagonal sum is 2a + 8. The other is a + a + 1 + 7. What shows they are equal?
options: 1 + 7 makes 8
2a makes 1 + 7
8 makes 1 and 7
a makes 2a + 8

why.2a makes 1 + 7: The two a terms are equal; 1 and 7 supply the missing 8.
why.8 makes 1 and 7: The child treats the final 8 as making both smaller numbers.
why.a makes 2a + 8: The child wrongly thinks a and 2a are the same number.

activities.explanation: Adding 1 and 7 gives 8, so both sums equal 2a + 8.

activities.prompt: The five-number calendar shape has centre a. A child says its total is 5 + a. Why is this wrong?
options: Five times a means 5a, not 5 + a.
The centre is multiplied by five, and one is then added.
The centre is not multiplied; it is only added once.
The word five means plus five, not times five.

why.The centre is multiplied by five, and on: This adds an extra one after finding five times the centre.
why.The centre is not multiplied; it is only: This leaves out the repeated copies of the centre number.

activities.explanation: The total is five times the centre, so it equals 5a.

activities.prompt: Step 5 needs 11 matchsticks. Each new step adds two. Which rule fits both facts?
options: Start with 3, then add 2 × (y – 1).
Start with 3, then add 2 × y.
Start with 2, then add 3 × (y – 1).
Start with 3, then add (2y – 1).

This counts one extra pair of sticks at the first step.
This swaps 3 and 2, changing both the start and the step size.
This moves the subtraction outside the multiplication.

activities.explanation: This is the stated rule and gives 11 at step 5.

activities.prompt: The matchstick expression is 3 + 2 × (y – 1). A child says it equals 2y + 3. Why is the child wrong?
options: 2 × (y – 1) is 2y – 2; adding 3 gives 2y + 1.
2 × (y – 1) is 2y + 2; adding 3 gives 2y + 5.
2 × (y – 1) is 2y – 3; adding 3 gives 2y.
2 × (y – 1) is 2y – 1; adding 3 gives 2y + 2.

why.2 × (y – 1) is 2y + 2; adding 3 gives 2y: This turns y – 1 into y + 1 inside the brackets.
why.2 × (y – 1) is 2y – 3; adding 3 gives 2y: This moves the outside 3 into the brackets.
why.2 × (y – 1) is 2y – 1; adding 3 gives 2y: This leaves out the subtraction of 2 from the doubled part.

activities.explanation: Doubling y and subtracting 2 gives 2y – 2, then adding 3 gives 2y + 1.

activities.context: Shabnam is three years older than Aftab. If a is Aftab’s age and s is Shabnam’s age, s is found by adding 3 to a, while a is found by subtracting 3 from s. At a shop, c coconuts and j kg of jaggery cost c × 35 + j × 60 in total. Shabnam is also arranging n letter-L shapes, and each L needs two matchsticks.
activities.prompt: If Aftab’s age a changes, which expression should Shabnam use to calculate her age s?

why.a – 3: Subtracting 3 would describe Aftab’s age from s, not Shabnam’s age from a.
why.a × 3: Multiplying by 3 does not follow the stated age relationship.
why.s – 3: This is the expression for Aftab’s age from Shabnam’s age, so it reverses the task.

activities.explanation: Shabnam’s age is found by adding 3 to Aftab’s age.

activities.context: Shabnam is three years older than Aftab. If a is Aftab’s age and s is Shabnam’s age, s is found by adding 3 to a, while a is found by subtracting 3 from s. At a shop, c coconuts and j kg of jaggery cost c × 35 + j × 60 in total. Shabnam is also arranging n letter-L shapes, and each L needs two matchsticks.
activities.prompt: Which expression tells Shabnam how many matchsticks she needs for n letter-L shapes?

why.2 + n: This adds 2 once rather than counting two for every L.
why.n – 2: Subtracting 2 does not count the matchsticks needed.

activities.explanation: The matchstick total is 2 times the number of Ls.

activities.prompt: Explain why s = a + 3 and a = s – 3 describe the same age relationship.
activities.answer: Shabnam’s age is found by adding 3 to Aftab’s age, so the expression for s is a + 3. Aftab’s age is 3 less than Shabnam’s age, so the expression for a is s – 3. The two expressions describe the same age relationship in opposite directions.
points: a represents Aftab’s age.
s represents Shabnam’s age.
Adding 3 to a gives s, while subtracting 3 from s gives a.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student records an age as s = a + 3. Swapping and grouping the terms do not change the expression’s value. A multiple of (a + 3) can be expanded as the sum of the multiples. In the second expression, all terms are numbers. Its brackets have a negative sign outside them. Each term containing a multiplication sign must become a number before addition. Replacing a by 23 gives s = 23 + 3 = 26 years.
activities.prompt: The student writes a multiple of the sum as m × (a + 3). Which expression should replace it?
options: m × a + m × 3
m + a + 3
m × a + 3

why.m + a + 3: This adds m directly instead of multiplying each term.
why.m × a + 3: It multiplies only a and fails to multiply 3 by m.
why.(m + a) × 3: It changes the grouping instead of applying the multiple to both terms.

activities.explanation: A multiple of a sum equals the sum of the multiples.

activities.context: A student records an age as s = a + 3. Swapping and grouping the terms do not change the expression’s value. A multiple of (a + 3) can be expanded as the sum of the multiples. In the second expression, all terms are numbers. Its brackets have a negative sign outside them. Each term containing a multiplication sign must become a number before addition. Replacing a by 23 gives s = 23 + 3 = 26 years.
activities.prompt: In the second expression, the student removes the brackets from −(a + 3). Which expression should remain?

why.−a + 3: It applies the outside negative sign to only one term.
why.a − 3: It removes the outside negative sign and changes the sign of 3.
why.a + 3: It keeps the original terms but loses the negative sign.

activities.explanation: Removing the brackets keeps the negative sign on both a and 3.

activities.prompt: Explain why swapping and grouping do not change the value of s = a + 3, and how to find its value when a is replaced by 23.
activities.answer: Swapping and grouping terms only change how the expression is arranged, so its value stays the same. After replacing a by 23, the expression becomes 23 + 3. Adding the two terms gives s = 26 years, whether the terms are written as a + 3 or 3 + a.
points: Swapping changes the order, not the value.
Grouping changes the arrangement, not the value.
Replace a by 23.
Calculate 23 + 3 = 26 years.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class examines a number sequence. Its first terms are 4, 8, and 12. The twenty-ninth term is 4 × 29, and the term at position n is 4 times n. Leaving out the multiplication sign makes an expression shorter, with the number before the letter. One learner writes 7k. With k set to 4, the result is 28. Elsewhere, 5m + 3 is checked with m set to 2, giving 13.
activities.prompt: A student needs a shortened expression for the term at any position n. What should the student write?
options: 4n
n4

why.29n: 29n would use the twenty-ninth position for every term.
why.4 + n: 4 + n shows addition rather than omitted multiplication.
why.n4: n4 places the number after the letter, but the number must come first.

activities.explanation: The term at position n is 4 times n.

activities.context: A class examines a number sequence. Its first terms are 4, 8, and 12. The twenty-ninth term is 4 × 29, and the term at position n is 4 times n. Leaving out the multiplication sign makes an expression shorter, with the number before the letter. One learner writes 7k. With k set to 4, the result is 28. Elsewhere, 5m + 3 is checked with m set to 2, giving 13.
activities.prompt: A checker sees 5m + 3 with m = 2 and the result 13. Which explanation is correct?
options: Calculate 5 × m first, then add 3; the result is 13.
Calculate 5 + m first, then add 3; the result is 13.
Calculate 5 × 3 first, then add m; the result is 13.
Calculate 5 + m first, then multiply by 3; the result is 13.

why.Calculate 5 + m first, then add 3; the r: Adding m changes the multiplication into addition.
why.Calculate 5 × 3 first, then add m; the r: The 3 in 5m + 3 is added after 5m; it is not a multiplier.
why.Calculate 5 + m first, then multiply by: The expression does not ask for addition before multiplication.

activities.explanation: The expression 5m means 5 × m, so multiplication comes first.

activities.prompt: Explain why 4 × 29 represents the twenty-ninth term and how its shortened form is written.
activities.answer: The twenty-ninth term has n equal to 29 because n shows a position. The nth term is 4 times n, so the term is 4 × 29. Leaving out the multiplication sign puts the number before the letter and gives 4n.
points: n shows a position in the sequence
The twenty-ninth position has n = 29
The nth term is 4 times n
The shortened form has the number before the letter
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A rectangular garden has length l and breadth b. To find its perimeter p, a student adds the sides: p = l + b + l + b. She then writes p = 2l + 2b, so both methods give the same perimeter. If l = 3 and b = 4, each method gives 14. In a pencil task, she adds c for each of the three parts 5 + 3 + 10, giving 18c. The expression 18c + 11d has unlike terms. Two smaller areas, 4v and 3v, add to 7v.
activities.prompt: If the student checks the perimeter using both expressions when l = 3 and b = 4, what should she conclude?
options: The two forms must both equal 14.
The first form gives 14, but the second gives a different value.
Only the simplified form can be used for a perimeter.
The perimeter changes when the expression is simplified.

why.The first form gives 14, but the second: Simplifying does not change the value.
why.Only the simplified form can be used for: The second form still includes both l and b.
why.The perimeter changes when the expressio: Rewriting an expression does not change its value.

activities.explanation: Both expressions represent the same perimeter.

activities.context: A rectangular garden has length l and breadth b. To find its perimeter p, a student adds the sides: p = l + b + l + b. She then writes p = 2l + 2b, so both methods give the same perimeter. If l = 3 and b = 4, each method gives 14. In a pencil task, she adds c for each of the three parts 5 + 3 + 10, giving 18c. The expression 18c + 11d has unlike terms. Two smaller areas, 4v and 3v, add to 7v.
activities.prompt: What should the student do with 18c + 11d when checking whether it can be simplified?
options: Keep the two unlike terms separate because their letter-numbers differ.
Combine them into one term even though the letters differ.
Replace them with 7v because all terms can be combined.
Combine them into 18c because the 11d term can be ignored.

why.Combine them into one term even though t: Unlike terms should not be combined.
why.Replace them with 7v because all terms c: 7v comes from combining the like terms 4v and 3v.

activities.explanation: Different letter-numbers make the terms unlike.

activities.prompt: Explain why l + b + l + b and 2l + 2b give the same perimeter value.
activities.answer: The original expression adds the two lengths and the two breadths. Grouping the two lengths gives 2l, and grouping the two breadths gives 2b. Therefore, l + b + l + b and 2l + 2b have the same value.
points: The two lengths are added together.
The two breadths are added together.
Regrouping does not change the value.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the position formulas for Designs A, B, and C are different.
activities.answer: The nth occurrence of Design B is at 3n − 1 because it is one less than a multiple of 3. The nth occurrence of Design A is two less than a multiple of 3, while the nth occurrence of Design C is at the multiple of 3. These differences explain the three position formulas.
points: Design B is one less than a multiple of 3.
Design A is two less than a multiple of 3.
Design C is at a multiple of 3.
The formulas are 3n – 1, 3n – 2, and 3n.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the two diagonal sums are equal for any value of a.
activities.answer: The diagonal sums are a + a + 8 and a + a + 1 + 7. The first simplifies to 2a + 8. The second also simplifies to 2a + 8, because 1 + 7 equals 8. Therefore, the diagonal sums are equal for any value of a.
points: Writes both diagonal-sum expressions.
Simplifies each expression to 2a + 8.
Explains that 1 + 7 equals 8.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

lessons.title: 5.1 Across the Line

activities.prompt: Can you solve the missing-angle puzzle created by two crossing lines?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet at One Point
activities.body: Intersecting lines meet at one point on a plane surface. They form four angles. Angles beside each other are adjacent angles. When they make a straight line, they add up to 180 degrees. Angles across the crossing are opposite angles, and they are equal. A clear justification of a mathematical statement is called a proof.
keyPoints: Intersecting lines meet at one point.
They form four angles.
Opposite angles are equal.
activities.explanation: You have met the main ideas for lines and angles.

activities.prompt: Angle a measures 90 degrees. Angle b is adjacent to angle a, and together they form a straight line. What is the measure of angle b in degrees?
steps: Angle a is 90 degrees.
Angles a and b form a straight line, so their measures add to 180 degrees.
180 - 90 = 90, so angle b is 90 degrees.

gen.template: Angle a measures {a} degrees. Angle b is adjacent to angle a, and together they form a straight line. What is the measure of angle b in degrees?
steps: Angle a is {a} degrees.
Angles a and b form a straight line, so their measures add to 180 degrees.
180 - {a} = {answer}, so angle b is {answer} degrees.
gen.hint: Use the fact that adjacent angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

lessons.title: 5.5 Transversals and 5.6 Corresponding Angles

activities.prompt: How can one angle reveal whether two lines are parallel?

activities.title: Meet Transversals
activities.body: A transversal intersects two different lines and forms eight angles. One line gets one angle set, and the other gets another. These angles make four vertically opposite pairs. Each pair has equal angles. There are at most four different measures. Corresponding pairs include 1 and 5. Also, 2 and 6, 3 and 7, and 4 and 8 are corresponding pairs. Equal corresponding angles show that the lines are parallel.
keyPoints: A transversal intersects two different lines.
The eight angles make four vertically opposite pairs.
Equal corresponding angles show that the lines are parallel.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas for transversals and corresponding angles.

activities.prompt: A transversal crosses two lines. Angle 1 measures 20 degrees. What measure, in degrees, is the vertically opposite angle to angle 1?
steps: Angle 1 is given as 20 degrees.
Vertically opposite angles are equal, so angle 3 also measures 20 degrees.
Therefore, the vertically opposite angle measures 20 degrees.

activities.body: Equal corresponding angles give a clear clue about two lines. If the angles are equal, the lines are parallel. activities.prompt: Explain why two intersecting lines form four angles and how the opposite angles are related.

Vertically opposite angles are equal to each other, so each angle in one opposite pair has the same measure as its partner.

Two intersecting lines form four angles.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.

activities.prompt: Can you uncover what each child’s number reveals about their height?

activities.title: Numbers Describe an Arrangement
activities.body: In this lesson, each child says how many children in front are taller than them. Children 1, 2, 4 and 6 call out 0. Child 3 calls out 1. Children 5 and 7 call out 3. The largest possible number in a group of 8 people is 7. Numbers can show how a sequence is arranged without showing the actual numbers.
keyPoints: Each child counts taller children in front.
The called numbers describe the shown arrangement.
Numbers can describe an arrangement without showing the actual numbers.
activities.explanation: The calls help us understand how the children are arranged.

activities.prompt: There are 8 children in a group. What is the largest possible number of children in front of the last child who can be taller than that child?
steps: The last child has 7 children in front of them.
Every child in front could be taller than the last child.
Therefore, 7 = 7 is the largest possible number.

Therefore, {ahead} = {answer} is the largest possible number.

A caller can count only children who are already ahead.

So the largest possible number in the sequence is 7.

steps: A child's call-out counts the taller children in front.
The number called out is 2.
Therefore, 2 = 2 children in front are taller.

activities.title: Even Numbers and Odd Numbers
activities.body: Even numbers can be arranged in pairs without leftovers. Odd numbers cannot be arranged completely in pairs. An odd number is one more than a collection of pairs. Parity means being even or odd. The sum of two odd numbers is always even. The sum of three odd numbers cannot be arranged in pairs. Two consecutive numbers contain one even number and one odd number.
keyPoints: Even numbers can be arranged in pairs.
Odd numbers have one number left over.
Parity means being even or odd.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you spot even and odd numbers.

Therefore, all the pencils can be arranged in pairs without leftovers.

activities.title: Odd, Even and Parity
activities.body: A grid’s parity can be odd or even. A 3 × 3 grid has 9 small squares, so it is odd. A 3 × 4 grid has 12 small squares, so it is even. One even dimension makes a grid even. Both odd dimensions make it odd. The formulas 2n and 2n – 1 give the nth even and odd numbers. Also, 3n + 4 can have either parity.
keyPoints: A 3 × 3 grid is odd; a 3 × 4 grid is even.
One even dimension means an even grid.
2n gives the nth even number; 2n – 1 gives the nth odd number.
activities.explanation: Even and odd patterns follow clear rules.

lessons.title: Grids and Magic Squares

activities.prompt: What secret pattern could make a grid feel like magic?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What makes a magic square?
activities.body: Think of a grid as rows and columns. A magic square has the same sum in every row, column and diagonal. A diagonal joins opposite corners. The common sum is called the magic sum. For a square using 1 to 9, the magic sum is 15, and the centre is 5. The numbers 1 and 9 cannot sit in corners.
keyPoints: Rows, columns and diagonals have equal sums.
The common sum is called the magic sum.
A magic sum of 15 needs 5 in the centre.
activities.explanation: A magic square keeps equal sums in its rows, columns and diagonals.

activities.prompt: A 3 × 3 grid uses 1 to 9 once. Its row and column circles show 5 and 26. Can the grid work?
steps: Every row and column contains three different numbers.
The smallest possible line sum is 6, so 5 is impossible.
The largest possible line sum is 24, so 26 is impossible.
Both circled sums fail, so the grid cannot work.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which rule describes a magic square?
options: Rows, columns and diagonals have equal sums.
Rows and columns have equal sums, not diagonals.
Rows have equal sums, but columns do not.
Columns have equal sums, but rows do not.
activities.explanation: The defining rule includes rows, columns and diagonals. Each has the same sum.

activities.prompt: The circled numbers give the sums of only the rows.
activities.explanation: They give the sums of the matching rows and columns.

activities.prompt: A magic square using 1 to 9 has a magic sum of ______.
activities.hint: Remember the special sum for this square.
activities.explanation: A magic square using 1 to 9 must have a magic sum of 15.

why.The rows must use three repeated numbers: Equal row sums do not require repeated numbers in each row.
why.The columns must have different sums fro: The rule asks for equal column sums, not different ones.
A sum of 34 applies to the Chautīsā Yantra, not every grid.

activities.explanation: A magic square needs equal sums for rows, columns, and diagonals.

activities.prompt: The first recorded 4 × 4 magic square was found at the Pārśhvanath Jain temple in Khajuraho. What does this show about magic squares?
options: Magic squares are not limited to 3 × 3 grids.
Magic squares must all have exactly 3 × 3 cells.
Magic squares must all have magic sum 15.
Magic squares cannot have equal row, column, and diagonal sums.

why.Magic squares must all have exactly 3 ×: This wrongly assumes that magic squares can only be 3 × 3.
why.Magic squares must all have magic sum 15: The Chautīsā Yantra is magic with magic sum 34.
why.Magic squares cannot have equal row, col: Equal row, column, and diagonal sums are exactly what magic squares need.

activities.explanation: A recorded 4 × 4 magic square proves that size is possible.

lessons.title: Virahāṅka–Fibonacci Numbers

activities.prompt: How did ancient poets help mathematicians find a special number pattern?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Numbers Connected with Poetry
activities.body: Virahāṅka numbers first appeared in work connected with poetry. In Sanskrit, Prakrit and other Indian poetry, each syllable is long or short. A short syllable lasts one beat. A long syllable lasts exactly twice as long, so it lasts two beats. Virahāṅka gave his counting method around 700 CE. Fibonacci wrote about these numbers in 1202 CE.
keyPoints: The numbers first appeared in work connected with poetry.
Short syllables last one beat, while long syllables last two.
Virahāṅka shared his method around 700 CE.
activities.explanation: You can see how poetry, counting and mathematics are closely linked.

activities.prompt: A poem contains 4 short syllables, and each short syllable lasts one beat. How many beats does the poem contain?
steps: Each short syllable lasts one beat.
There are 4 short syllables in the poem.
One beat for each syllable gives 1 x 4 = 4, so the answer is 4 beats.

gen.template: A poem contains {n} short syllables, and each short syllable lasts one beat. How many beats does the poem contain?
steps: Each short syllable lasts one beat.
There are {n} short syllables in the poem.
One beat for each syllable gives 1 x {n} = {total_beats}, so the answer is {answer} beats.
gen.hint: Count one beat for each short syllable.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A short syllable lasts one beat. A long syllable lasts two beats. A poem has 3 short and 2 long syllables. How many beats does it have?
steps: Each short syllable adds 1 beat, because a short syllable lasts one beat.
Each long syllable adds 2 beats, because a long syllable lasts two beats.
Three short syllables add 3 beats, and two long syllables add 4 beats.
The poem has 3 + 4 = 7 beats, so its rhythm lasts 7 beats.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A poem contains 4 long syllables, and each long syllable lasts two beats. How many beats do the long syllables contain?
activities.explanation: Each long syllable lasts two beats. There are 4 long syllables in the poem. Two beats for each syllable gives 2 x 4 = 8, so the answer is 8 beats.
steps: Each long syllable lasts two beats.
There are 4 long syllables in the poem.
Two beats for each syllable gives 2 x 4 = 8, so the answer is 8 beats.
activities.hint: Multiply the number of long syllables by the two beats in each one.

gen.template: A poem contains {n} long syllables, and each long syllable lasts two beats. How many beats do the long syllables contain?
steps: Each long syllable lasts two beats.
There are {n} long syllables in the poem.
Two beats for each syllable gives 2 x {n} = {total_beats}, so the answer is {answer} beats.
gen.hint: Multiply the number of long syllables by the two beats in each one.
wrongWhy: You counted each long syllable as only one beat.
You added one extra beat instead of two beats for every syllable.
You used three beats for each long syllable.

why.4: You counted each long syllable as only one beat.
why.5: You added one extra beat instead of two beats for every syllable.
why.12: You used three beats for each long syllable.

The rhythm is repeated 6 times.

activities.prompt: Virahāṅka gave his counting method around 700 CE, and Fibonacci wrote about these numbers in 1202 CE. A student says the two dates are 200 years apart. How many years does the student's claim fall short of the correct difference?

two short and one long
three short syllables
three long syllables

derived: one short and two long = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 beats

activities.prompt: Piṅgala lived around 300 BCE. Virahāṅka gave his counting method around 700 CE. Fibonacci wrote about these numbers in 1202 CE. Put these three people in time order from earliest to latest.
options: Piṅgala first, then Virahāṅka, then Fibonacci
Virahāṅka first, then Piṅgala, then Fibonacci

why.Fibonacci first, then Piṅgala, then Vira: This places the latest known time before the earlier times.

activities.explanation: This order starts with 300 BCE and then follows 700 CE and 1202 CE.

activities.prompt: A short syllable lasts one beat. A long syllable lasts exactly twice as long. A child says a long syllable should count as one beat. What correction is needed?

It should count as two beats, because all rhythms have two beats.
It should count as three beats, because it is longer than short.

why.It should count as one beat, because all: This wrongly says that long and short syllables last equally.
why.It should count as two beats, because al: This gives two beats but uses an unsupported reason.
why.It should count as three beats, because: This adds a third beat, but no fact gives that rule.

activities.explanation: This uses the correct rule that a long syllable lasts twice as long.

activities.prompt: Virahāṅka numbers first appeared in work connected with poetry. In Sanskrit, Prakrit and other Indian poetry, each syllable is long or short. What best explains why these numbers link poetry and mathematics?

They count the number of letters in every poem.
They count the number of artists who used poetry.

why.They count how many poems were written e: This counts poems by time, which the facts do not describe.
why.They count the number of letters in ever: This counts letters instead of syllable lengths and beats.
why.They count the number of artists who use: This counts people instead of the rhythms in poetry.

activities.explanation: This connects the long and short syllables in poetry with counting beats.

activities.prompt: Can you uncover the hidden digits behind a letter puzzle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Letters Can Hide Digits
activities.body: A cryptarithm replaces digits with letters. Each letter stands for one particular digit from 0 to 9. Cryptarithms are also called alphametics. When a one-digit number is added to itself twice, the sum can have two digits. Its units digit matches the original digit. A number like K2 can become HMM when added to itself.
keyPoints: Letters replace digits.
Each letter has one digit.
Cryptarithms are also called alphametics.
activities.explanation: Letters act as disguises for particular digits.

activities.prompt: A child sees T = 5 and UT = 15 in a cryptarithm. How can the child check it?
steps: T is 5 because the first example gives that value.
Adding 5 to itself twice means using three copies.
Because 5 + 5 + 5 gives 15, the sum matches UT.
The units digit is 5, so it matches T.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Reading Cryptarithm Examples
activities.body: When a one-digit number is added to itself twice, the sum can have two digits. The units digit of the sum matches the original digit. In the first example, T is 5 and UT is 15. Another cryptarithm adds K2 to itself to make HMM. In the final cryptarithm, U is 9, T is 1 and A is 0.
keyPoints: The units digit stays the same.
Different examples use different letters.
Each letter represents one digit.
activities.explanation: These examples show how letters can hide digits in sums.

activities.prompt: What does a cryptarithm do?
options: It replaces digits with letters.
It replaces letters with words.
It changes numbers into sounds.
It removes digits from numbers.
activities.explanation: A cryptarithm replaces digits with letters.

activities.prompt: Each letter can represent a different digit every time it appears.
activities.explanation: Each letter represents one particular digit from 0 to 9.

activities.prompt: Cryptarithms are also called ______.
activities.hint: The answer begins with a.
activities.explanation: Alphametics is another name for cryptarithms.

activities.prompt: Which part matches the original digit in the sum?
options: The units digit
The tens digit
The hundreds digit
The whole sum
activities.explanation: The units digit of the two-digit sum matches the original digit.

activities.prompt: Match each cryptarithm part to its value.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives T as 5, UT as 15, U as 9 and A as 0.

activities.prompt: In the final cryptarithm, what is U + T + A?
activities.explanation: Use the digits U = 9, T = 1 and A = 0. They add to 10.

activities.prompt: Put these Virahāṅka numbers in increasing order.
activities.explanation: The numbers increase from 987 to 1597 to 2584 to 4181.

activities.prompt: T is 5, and UT is 15 in the first cryptarithm. Which calculation explains UT?

why.5 + 5 = 15: This uses only two copies and misses the second extra copy.
why.5 + 15 + 5 = 15: This adds UT again instead of using three copies of T.
why.15 + 15 + 5 = 15: This starts with UT instead of using three copies of T.

activities.explanation: This uses three copies because a number is added to itself twice.

activities.prompt: In the final cryptarithm, U is 9 and T is 1. Also, A is 0. A child writes T as 9. Which repair follows the rule?
options: Restore T as 1 because its digit is fixed.
Keep T as 9 because U uses 9.
Change U to 1 because T uses 1.
Change A to 9 because U uses 9.

A letter cannot copy another letter's digit in this puzzle.
This changes a correct digit because T uses 1.
This changes A even though A's digit is already given as 0.

activities.explanation: Each letter keeps one particular digit, so T must remain 1.

An eighth child joins the back of the line and wonders which number to call.
activities.prompt: If the eighth child is taller than all seven children ahead, which is the largest number they can call?

why.6: Six is possible, but it is not the largest possible count.
why.3: Three is possible, but it is not the largest possible count.

activities.context: At a school activity, seven children stand in a line. Each child says how many children in front are taller than them. activities.prompt: If the eighth child moves to the front and is taller than every original child, what happens to the original children's counts?
options: Each original child's count increases by one.
Each original child's count stays the same.
Each original child's count becomes zero.
Each original child's count increases by two.

why.Each original child's count stays the sa: This ignores the new taller child standing in front.
why.Each original child's count becomes zero: Moving a taller child to the front does not remove any taller children.

activities.prompt: Explain how the calls describe the line without giving the children's exact heights.
activities.answer: Each call gives the number of taller children standing ahead of that child. For example, child 5's call of 3 means exactly three of the four children ahead are taller. The calls show comparisons within the line, but they do not state anyone's exact height.
points: A call counts taller children in front.
Child 5 has exactly three taller children ahead.
The calls describe relative comparisons.
Exact heights are not stated.

activities.prompt: Explain how pairing shows the difference between even numbers and odd numbers, and what happens when two consecutive numbers are added.
activities.answer: Even numbers can be arranged completely in pairs, with nothing left over. Odd numbers cannot be arranged completely in pairs; an odd number is one more than a collection of pairs. Two consecutive numbers contain one even number and one odd number, so their sum always has odd parity.
points: Says that even numbers leave no leftovers.
Says that odd numbers cannot be paired completely.
Explains that an odd number has one more than a collection of pairs.
Explains the parity of the sum of consecutive numbers.

It will have odd parity, with 9 small squares.

why.It will have even parity, with 9 small s: The new grid has 12 small squares, not 9.
why.It will have odd parity, with 12 small s: One dimension is 4, which is even, so the grid has even parity.
why.It will have odd parity, with 9 small sq: The new count is 12, and one even dimension makes the grid even.

Both dimensions odd gives odd parity; one even dimension gives even parity.

activities.prompt: Which information should the student put on labels for the 3 × 3 magic square and the Chautīsā Yantra?
options: The magic square has a magic sum of 15; every row, column and diagonal of the Chautīsā Yantra adds to 34.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a magic square and its magic sum. Include what the magic sum must be for a 3 × 3 square using 1 to 9.

The magic sum for a 3 × 3 square using 1 to 9 is 15.

lessons.title: Triangle Basics and Equilateral Triangles

activities.prompt: What makes a triangle with perfectly matching sides so special?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Parts of a Triangle
activities.body: A triangle is the most basic closed shape in the chapter. It has three corner points, called vertices. Its sides join pairs of vertices. The sides at the corners form three angles. In triangle ABC, the angles are CAB, ABC and BCA. You may also call them A, B and C. An equilateral triangle is the most symmetric triangle. It has three equal sides.
keyPoints: A triangle has three vertices.
Its sides join pairs of vertices.
It has three angles.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides.
activities.explanation: These are the main parts and names you need.

activities.prompt: Each of the three sides of an equilateral triangle is 2 cm long. What is the total length of its three sides in cm?
steps: The length of each side is 2 cm.
An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, so add 2 cm that many times.

gen.template: Each of the three sides of an equilateral triangle is {s} cm long. What is the total length of its three sides in cm?
steps: The length of each side is {sideLength} cm.
An equilateral triangle has {sidesEach} equal sides, so add {sideLength} cm that many times.
{sidesEach} x {sideLength} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Add the length of one side three times.
wrongWhy: You counted only two sides.
You counted four sides instead of three.
You counted only one side.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A child plans the chapter's most basic closed shape. Should each of its three sides be 4 cm long?
steps: The most basic closed shape in the chapter is a triangle.
The chapter asks for an equilateral triangle with 4 cm sides.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides.
Therefore, all three sides should measure 4 cm.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Can three lengths always make a triangle?

activities.title: The Triangle Inequality
activities.body: The direct straight-line path is shorter than a path through a third point. For triangle lengths, compare each length with the sum of the other two lengths. This condition is called the triangle inequality. A triangle exists whenever the lengths satisfy it. The set 3, 4, 5 satisfies it. The set 10, 15, 30 does not.
keyPoints: Compare each length with the sum of the others.
The rule is called the triangle inequality.
A triangle exists when the given lengths satisfy the rule.
activities.explanation: Compare every length before deciding whether a triangle exists.

activities.prompt: A triangle has side lengths 2 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm, where 3 cm is the longest side. By how many cm is the sum of the two shorter sides greater than the longest side?
steps: The two shorter lengths are 2 cm and 2 cm, and the longest is 3 cm.
The sum of the shorter lengths is 4 cm, which is greater than 3 cm.
4 cm - 3 cm = 1 cm.

activities.title: Comparing Circles
activities.body: The circles touch when the two smaller lengths add to the longest length. If their sum is less than the longest length, the circles do not intersect. Here, intersect means the circles cross. If their sum is more than the longest length, the circles intersect. Compare the sum with the longest length.
keyPoints: When the sum equals the longest length, the circles touch.
When the sum is less, the circles do not intersect.
When the sum is more, the circles intersect.
activities.explanation: The sum of the smaller lengths decides the circle outcome.

gen.hint: The height can change when the base changes, so add both measured heights.

activities.prompt: A triangle has an exterior angle of 110°. How many degrees larger is this exterior angle than the interior angle beside it?
steps: The exterior angle measures 110 degrees.
Its adjacent interior angle measures 180 - 110 = 70 degrees.
110 - 70 = 40 degrees.

gen.template: A triangle has an exterior angle of {e}°. How many degrees larger is this exterior angle than the interior angle beside it?
steps: The exterior angle measures {e} degrees.
Its adjacent interior angle measures 180 - {e} = {interior} degrees.
{e} - {interior} = {answer} degrees.
gen.hint: First find the adjacent interior angle, then subtract it from the exterior angle.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.title: Order the Construction
activities.prompt: Put these actions in order to construct the perpendicular.
items: Slide the set square along the ruler
Drop a perpendicular from A to it
activities.explanation: Extend BC, slide the set square along the ruler, and draw the perpendicular from A.

activities.prompt: A set square is first slid 6 cm along a ruler and then slid 6 cm farther along the same ruler. What is the total distance slid, in cm?
activities.explanation: The first slide covers 6 cm. The second slide covers another 6 cm. 6 + 6 = 12 cm.
steps: The first slide covers 6 cm.
The second slide covers another 6 cm.
activities.hint: First find the distance after both slides, then state the total.

gen.template: A set square is first slid {d1} cm along a ruler and then slid {d2} cm farther along the same ruler. What is the total distance slid, in cm?
steps: The first slide covers {d1} cm.
The second slide covers another {d2} cm.
{d1} + {d2} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: First find the distance after both slides, then state the total.

activities.prompt: For three different choices of base, a triangular chart has heights of 3 cm, 6 cm, and 6 cm. What is the total length of all three altitudes, in cm?
activities.explanation: The three base choices give heights of 3 cm, 6 cm, and 6 cm. First, 3 + 6 = 9 cm. Then 9 + 6 = 15 cm.
steps: The three base choices give heights of 3 cm, 6 cm, and 6 cm.
First, 3 + 6 = 9 cm.
Then 9 + 6 = 15 cm.
activities.hint: First add the first two heights, then add the third height.

gen.template: For three different choices of base, a triangular chart has heights of {h1} cm, {h2} cm, and {h3} cm. What is the total length of all three altitudes, in cm?
steps: The three base choices give heights of {h1} cm, {h2} cm, and {h3} cm.
First, {h1} + {h2} = {first_two} cm.
Then {first_two} + {h3} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: First add the first two heights, then add the third height.

activities.prompt: A bicycle frame is a triangle. Its side BC is extended past C. How is angle ACD formed?
options: Between extended BC and side AC.
Between side AB and side AC.
Between extended BC and side AB.
Between side BC and perpendicular AD.

This uses two sides meeting at A, not the extended side.
This uses the wrong side, because ACD does not use AB.
This mixes the perpendicular segment into the angle.

activities.explanation: Because BC is extended, ACD is an exterior angle.

activities.prompt: A classroom model repeats the chapter's example. Angle ACD is 110°, and AD is perpendicular to BC. Which pair describes their roles?
options: ACD is exterior; AD is an altitude.
ACD is an altitude; AD is exterior.
ACD is a height; AD is a base.
ACD is a base; AD is a height.

This swaps the exterior angle and the perpendicular altitude.
This swaps the altitude and base, and calls the angle a height.
This swaps the angle and perpendicular segment with base and height roles.

activities.explanation: BC is extended to form ACD, and AD is perpendicular to BC.

activities.prompt: A triangular craft has AD perpendicular to BC. What should be done to obtain another altitude?
options: Draw a perpendicular from another vertex to its base.
Extend AD beyond BC to make another altitude.
Extend another side to make another altitude.
Join another vertex to any point on BC.

why.Extend AD beyond BC to make another alti: Extending the same altitude does not draw a perpendicular from another vertex.
why.Extend another side to make another alti: Extending a side forms an exterior angle, not another altitude.
An altitude must meet its base perpendicularly, not at any point.

activities.explanation: The other altitudes are perpendiculars from the other vertices.

lessons.title: Types of Triangles

activities.prompt: Which triangle shape is hiding in your classroom, and how can you tell?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Triangle Types
activities.body: Triangles can be grouped by their sides or their angles. By sides, equilateral triangles have equal sides. Isosceles triangles have two equal sides. Scalene triangles have three different side lengths. By angles, a right-angled triangle has one right angle. An obtuse-angled triangle has one obtuse angle. An acute-angled triangle has three acute angles.
keyPoints: Equilateral triangles have equal sides.
Isosceles triangles have two equal sides.
Scalene triangles have three different side lengths.
Angle types include right-angled, obtuse-angled and acute-angled.
activities.explanation: These groups help you describe triangles clearly.

activities.prompt: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of lengths 4 cm and 4 cm, and a third side of length 10 cm. What is the total length of the two equal sides, in cm?
steps: The two equal sides have lengths 4 cm and 4 cm.
The third side is not needed for this question.

gen.template: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of lengths {a} cm and {b} cm, and a third side of length {c} cm. What is the total length of the two equal sides, in cm?
steps: The two equal sides have lengths {a} cm and {b} cm.
The third side is not needed for this question.
{equal_total} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Add the lengths of the two equal sides.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A paper triangle has two equal sides and one right angle. What type is it?
steps: Two sides have equal length, so it is isosceles.
One angle is right, so it is right-angled.
Both clues apply, because one checks sides and one checks angles.
Therefore, the triangle is isosceles and right-angled.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: An equilateral triangle has sides of equal length.
activities.explanation: Yes. All sides of an equilateral triangle are equal.

activities.prompt: A scalene triangle has three different side lengths of 8 cm, 9 cm, and 10 cm. What is the sum of its three side lengths, in cm?
activities.explanation: The triangle has three different side lengths. Add the lengths of all three sides. 27 = 27 cm.
steps: The triangle has three different side lengths.
Add the lengths of all three sides.
activities.hint: Add all three different side lengths.

gen.template: A scalene triangle has three different side lengths of {a} cm, {b} cm, and {c} cm. What is the sum of its three side lengths, in cm?
steps: The triangle has three different side lengths.
Add the lengths of all three sides.
{perimeter} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Add all three different side lengths.

activities.prompt: A scalene triangle has sides of ______ different lengths.
activities.hint: Think of the number of different side lengths.
activities.explanation: Scalene triangles have sides of three different lengths.

activities.prompt: Which triangle has exactly one right angle?
options: Acute-angled
Obtuse-angled
Scalene
Right-angled
activities.explanation: A right-angled triangle has one right angle.

activities.prompt: A school poster shows a scalene triangle with side lengths 13 cm, 15 cm, and 7 cm. What is the sum of the three side lengths, in cm?
activities.explanation: The poster shows a triangle with three different side lengths. Add the three lengths to find their sum. 35 = 35 cm.
steps: The poster shows a triangle with three different side lengths.
Add the three lengths to find their sum.
activities.hint: Add all three side lengths.

gen.template: A school poster shows a scalene triangle with side lengths {a} cm, {b} cm, and {c} cm. What is the sum of the three side lengths, in cm?
steps: The poster shows a triangle with three different side lengths.
Add the three lengths to find their sum.
{perimeter} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: Add all three side lengths.

activities.prompt: A bus-stop route marker is triangular, with one obtuse angle of 117 degrees and two acute angles of 39 degrees and 8 degrees. What is the sum of the two acute angles, in degrees?
activities.explanation: The angle of 117 degrees is obtuse. The other two angles are acute, so add their measures. 47 = 47 degrees.
steps: The angle of 117 degrees is obtuse.
The other two angles are acute, so add their measures.
47 = 47 degrees.
activities.hint: Add the two acute angles and leave out the obtuse angle.

gen.template: A bus-stop route marker is triangular, with one obtuse angle of {a} degrees and two acute angles of {b} degrees and {c} degrees. What is the sum of the two acute angles, in degrees?
steps: The angle of {a} degrees is obtuse.
The other two angles are acute, so add their measures.
{acute_total} = {answer} degrees.
gen.hint: Add the two acute angles and leave out the obtuse angle.

activities.prompt: A triangular playground has side lengths 15 cm, 14 cm, and 16 cm, and all three sides are different. What is the total length of the playground's three sides, in cm?
steps: The side lengths 15 cm, 14 cm, and 16 cm are all different.
Because every side is different, add all three lengths.

gen.template: A triangular playground has side lengths {a} cm, {b} cm, and {c} cm, and all three sides are different. What is the total length of the playground's three sides, in cm?
steps: The side lengths {a} cm, {b} cm, and {c} cm are all different.
Because every side is different, add all three lengths.
{perimeter} = {answer} cm.
gen.hint: First identify that all three sides belong in the total, then add them.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: An acute-angled triangle has one obtuse angle.
activities.explanation: No. All three angles of an acute-angled triangle are acute.

activities.prompt: A paper triangle has two equal sides and one right angle. Its third side has a different length. What type is it?
options: It is isosceles and right-angled.
It is equilateral and right-angled.
It is scalene and acute-angled.
It is isosceles and obtuse-angled.

Equilateral needs all three sides equal, but only two are.
Scalene needs three different sides, but two sides match.
An obtuse angle is missing, so the obtuse label does not fit.

activities.explanation: Two equal sides and one right angle match both types.

activities.prompt: A toy frame is triangular. All three sides have equal lengths. All three angles are acute. What type is it?
options: It is equilateral and acute-angled.
It is scalene and acute-angled.
It is equilateral and right-angled.
It is scalene and obtuse-angled.

Scalene needs three different sides, but every side matches.
One right angle cannot fit because all three angles are acute.
Both scalene and obtuse conflict with the given facts.

activities.explanation: All three sides match, and all three angles are acute.

activities.prompt: A garden sign is triangular. Its three sides have different lengths. One angle is obtuse. What type is it?
options: It is scalene and obtuse-angled.
It is isosceles and right-angled.
It is equilateral and acute-angled.
It is scalene and acute-angled.

Two sides are not equal, and no right angle is given.
Equilateral conflicts with three different sides, and acute misses the obtuse angle.
Scalene is right, but the obtuse angle prevents the acute label.

activities.explanation: Three different sides mean scalene, and one obtuse angle means obtuse.

activities.prompt: A bookmark is triangular. Two sides have equal lengths. The third side has a different length. All three angles are acute. What type is it?
options: It is isosceles and acute-angled.
It is equilateral and acute-angled.
It is scalene and obtuse-angled.
It is isosceles and right-angled.

Equilateral needs all three sides equal, but the third is different.
Scalene and obtuse both fail the given side and angle facts.
Isosceles is right, but all acute angles exclude a right angle.

activities.explanation: Two equal sides mean isosceles, and all acute angles mean acute.

activities.prompt: A triangular badge has two equal sides. A child says, “It must be equilateral.” Which reply is best?
options: Two equal sides fit isosceles; three equal sides fit equilateral.
Two equal sides fit equilateral, because matching sides prove all match.
One right angle fits equilateral, because angles decide side lengths.
Different sides fit scalene, so two equal sides need not match.

why.Two equal sides fit equilateral, because: This confuses two equal sides with all three equal sides.
why.One right angle fits equilateral, becaus: This mixes an angle fact with a side-based classification.
why.Different sides fit scalene, so two equa: This reverses the meanings of equal sides and different sides.

activities.explanation: Two equal sides fit isosceles, while three equal sides fit equilateral.
